posts.title: What is your brain doing while you sleep?
posts.caption: Sleep runs in cycles of light, deep, and REM sleep, about 80-100 minutes each (NIH NHLBI). Deep sleep dominates early, REM later. #sleep #sleepscience #sleepcycle #healthtok #brain

slides.text: What is your brain doing while you sleep?

slides.label: The stages
slides.title: Sleep has light, deep, and REM stages
slides.body: Stage 1 is the transition into sleep, stage 2 is light sleep, and stage 3 is deep sleep. REM is when your eyes move rapidly and most dreaming happens.
slides.source: Source: NIH NHLBI, Stages of sleep

slides.label: Early night
slides.title: Deep sleep comes first
slides.body: You usually spend more time in deep sleep early in the night, so the first few hours matter.
slides.source: Source: NIH NHLBI, Stages of sleep

slides.label: Late night
slides.title: REM comes later
slides.body: You usually get more REM sleep later in the night, which is why cutting your sleep short tends to cut into REM.
slides.source: Source: NIH NHLBI, Stages of sleep

slides.label: The pattern
slides.title: You cycle through it 4 to 6 times
slides.body: A full cycle takes roughly 80 to 100 minutes. Most people go through four to six cycles a night.
slides.source: Source: NIH NHLBI, Stages of sleep

slides.text: Better sleep is a skill. Get one tip a day.

posts.title: Alcohol helps you sleep? Here's what the research says
posts.caption: Alcohol can shorten the time to fall asleep, but it tends to cut REM sleep and disrupt the second half of the night (Ebrahim et al., 2013). #sleep #alcohol #sleepscience #healthtok #sleeptips

slides.text: Alcohol helps you sleep

slides.label: The upside
slides.title: It can help you fall asleep faster
slides.body: Across studies, alcohol shortened the time it took to fall asleep at all doses tested.
slides.source: Source: Ebrahim et al., Alcohol Clin Exp Res, 2013

slides.label: The trade
slides.title: More deep sleep early, less REM
slides.body: Most studies found more deep sleep in the first half of the night and less REM sleep at moderate and high doses.
slides.source: Source: Ebrahim et al., Alcohol Clin Exp Res, 2013

slides.label: The cost
slides.title: The second half of the night gets worse
slides.body: The review found more disrupted sleep in the second half of the night, which offsets the early benefit.
slides.source: Source: Ebrahim et al., Alcohol Clin Exp Res, 2013

slides.label: So what
slides.title: Fast to fall asleep is not the same as good sleep
slides.body: You may drop off quickly and still get sleep that is lighter and more broken than usual.

slides.text: Better sleep is a skill. Get one tip a day.

posts.title: Can you catch up on lost sleep on the weekend?
posts.caption: In a small lab study, weekend recovery sleep did not prevent metabolic disruption from a week of short sleep (Depner et al., 2019). Consistency beats cramming. #sleep #sleepdebt #sleepscience #healthtok #sleeptips

slides.text: Can you catch up on lost sleep on the weekend?
slides.sub: One lab study says not fully

slides.label: The study
slides.title: Short weeknights, then a weekend to sleep in
slides.body: In a small lab study, people slept about 5 hours a night on weekdays, were allowed to sleep in on the weekend, then went back to 5 hours.
slides.source: Source: Depner et al., Current Biology, 2019

slides.label: The result
slides.title: Weekend recovery sleep did not prevent metabolic disruption
slides.body: Insulin sensitivity still dropped. The recovery group's body rhythms were also disrupted when short sleep resumed.
slides.source: Source: Depner et al., Current Biology, 2019

slides.label: Takeaway
slides.title: Sleeping in may help you feel better, but it may not undo a short week
slides.body: It is one small study, but it points the same way: steady sleep every night beats cramming it into the weekend.

slides.text: Better sleep is a skill. Get one tip a day.

posts.title: Your bedroom may be too warm for good sleep
posts.caption: Your body cools down to fall asleep, and a bedroom around 65-68F (18-20C) supports that (Sleep Foundation). #sleeptips #sleepscore #sleephygiene #sleep #healthtok

slides.text: Your bedroom may be too warm for good sleep

slides.label: Your body clock
slides.title: Your body cools itself to fall asleep
slides.body: Your temperature starts dropping about two hours before you sleep and keeps falling until the early morning.
slides.source: Source: Sleep Foundation, best bedroom temperature

slides.label: The target
slides.title: Aim for 65–68°F (18–20°C)
slides.body: That range works with your body's natural cooling instead of against it.
slides.source: Source: Sleep Foundation, best bedroom temperature

slides.label: Too warm
slides.title: A hot room interferes with cooling
slides.body: It can disrupt sleep quality and cut into time in the restorative stages of sleep.
slides.source: Source: Sleep Foundation, best bedroom temperature

slides.label: Try this
slides.title: Turn it down before bed
slides.body: Lower the thermostat an hour before bedtime, use lighter bedding, or run a fan. Then watch your sleep score trend.

slides.text: Better sleep is a skill. Get one tip a day.

posts.title: What's actually in your sleep score?
posts.caption: Sleep scores usually blend duration, stages, timing, and restlessness. Each brand weights them differently, so compare your own trend. #sleepscore #sleeptracker #sleep #sleepscience #healthtok

slides.text: What is actually in your sleep score?

slides.title: Duration
slides.body: Adults should get 7 or more hours on a regular basis. Most scores start here.
slides.source: Source: AASM and SRS consensus statement, 2015

slides.title: Sleep stages
slides.body: Trackers estimate your light, deep, and REM sleep. Deep sleep comes earlier in the night and REM later, and these are estimates, not lab measurements.
slides.source: Source: NIH NHLBI, Stages of sleep

slides.title: Timing and consistency
slides.body: Going to bed and waking at similar times each day tends to count in your favor.

slides.title: Heart rate and HRV
slides.body: Many trackers include nighttime heart rate and heart rate variability. Both vary a lot from person to person, so watch your own trend.

slides.title: Restlessness
slides.body: Wake-ups and movement during the night can pull a score down, even if total time in bed looks fine.

slides.text: Better sleep is a skill. Get one tip a day.

posts.title: You need exactly 8 hours of sleep. Do you?
posts.caption: The expert guideline is 7 or more hours for adults, a minimum, not a fixed target (AASM and SRS). #sleep #sleepmyths #sleepscience #healthtok #sleeptips

slides.text: You need exactly 8 hours of sleep

slides.label: The guideline
slides.title: Adults should sleep 7 or more hours
slides.body: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society recommend 7 or more hours per night on a regular basis for adults 18 to 60.
slides.source: Source: AASM and SRS consensus statement, 2015

slides.label: The catch
slides.title: Seven is a floor, not a target
slides.body: "Seven or more" means some people will need 8 or 9. There is no single magic number.

slides.label: Check yourself
slides.title: Go by how you feel, with 7 as the floor
slides.body: If you wake up rested and stay alert through the day, you are probably in your range. If you are dragging, aim higher.

slides.text: Better sleep is a skill. Get one tip a day.

posts.title: A wind-down routine backed by research
posts.caption: Four evening habits with some research behind them: a warm shower, screens away, a to-do list, and a cool dark room. #sleeptips #sleephygiene #bedtimeroutine #sleep #healthtok

slides.text: A wind-down routine backed by research

slides.title: Take a warm shower or bath 1–2 hours before bed
slides.body: A review of studies found water around 104–109°F (40–43°C) at that time helped people fall asleep about 10 minutes sooner on average.
slides.source: Source: Haghayegh et al., Sleep Med Rev, 2019

slides.title: Put screens away about an hour before bed
slides.body: Occupational health guidance suggests avoiding computers an hour or so before bedtime, since light can signal your brain to stay alert.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, Training for Nurses on Shift Work

slides.title: Write tomorrow's to-do list
slides.body: In a sleep lab study, people who wrote a to-do list at bedtime fell asleep faster than those who wrote about what they had already done.
slides.source: Source: Scullin et al., J Exp Psychol Gen, 2018

slides.title: Keep the room cool and dark
slides.body: Aim for 65–68°F (18–20°C) and as dark as you can make it.
slides.source: Source: Sleep Foundation, best bedroom temperature

slides.text: Better sleep is a skill. Get one tip a day.

posts.title: How much light do you really need in the morning?
posts.caption: Daylight can be up to 10,000 lux outdoors, while bright office lighting rarely tops 500 (Sleep Foundation). Step outside soon after waking. #sleeptips #morninglight #sleepscore #sleep #healthtok

slides.text: How much light do you really need in the morning?

slides.label: The gap
slides.title: Outdoor light is far brighter than indoor light
slides.body: Direct sunlight can reach up to 10,000 lux. Even bright office lighting rarely goes above about 500 lux.
slides.source: Source: Sleep Foundation, light and sleep

slides.label: The habit
slides.title: Morning sunlight is a healthy light habit
slides.body: Getting morning sunlight and reducing evening light may help improve sleep quality.
slides.source: Source: Sleep Foundation, light and sleep

slides.label: Try this
slides.title: Step outside soon after you wake up
slides.body: Overcast skies are usually still brighter than indoor light, so a cloudy day still counts.

slides.text: Better sleep is a skill. Get one tip a day.

posts.title: Sleeping after a night shift: 5 tips from occupational health guidance
posts.caption: Tips from CDC NIOSH guidance for night workers. Only wear sunglasses home if someone else is driving. #nightshift #shiftwork #sleeptips #sleep #healthtok

slides.text: Sleeping after a night shift: 5 tips

slides.title: Go straight to bed when you get home
slides.body: The more sleep you get before 2 pm, the better rested you will be.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, Training for Nurses on Shift Work

slides.title: Spend as much time in bed as you can
slides.body: Night workers tend to get less and poorer sleep than day workers, so protect your sleep time.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, Training for Nurses on Shift Work

slides.title: Make the room very dark
slides.body: So dark you cannot see your hand in front of your face, or wear an eye mask. Blackout shades help.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, Training for Nurses on Shift Work

slides.title: Block noise and interruptions
slides.body: Use earplugs or white noise, and ask the people around you not to disturb your sleep.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, Training for Nurses on Shift Work

slides.title: Sunglasses on the way home, only if someone else drives
slides.body: Dark sunglasses can reduce the light that signals your body to be alert. Do not wear them while driving, since they can raise drowsiness and crash risk.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, Training for Nurses on Shift Work

slides.text: Better sleep is a skill. Get one tip a day.

posts.title: Two short nights raised appetite by 24% in one study
posts.caption: In a small study of 12 young men, two nights of 4-hour sleep lowered leptin, raised ghrelin, and increased appetite (Spiegel et al., 2004). #sleep #sleepscience #healthtok #hunger #sleeptips

slides.text: Two short nights raised appetite by 24%
slides.sub: One small study, and why tired days feel hungrier

slides.label: The study
slides.title: 12 men slept 4 hours for two nights
slides.body: Healthy young men in a University of Chicago study were compared after two nights of 4 hours vs two nights of 10 hours.
slides.source: Source: Spiegel et al., Ann Intern Med, 2004

slides.label: The hormones
slides.title: Fullness signal down, hunger signal up
slides.body: Leptin, which signals fullness, fell 18%. Ghrelin, which signals hunger, rose 28%. Overall appetite rose 24%.
slides.source: Source: Spiegel et al., Ann Intern Med, 2004

slides.label: The cravings
slides.title: Sweet, salty, and starchy foods won
slides.body: Desire for candy, cookies, chips, and bread rose, while desire for fruit, vegetables, and dairy rose much less.
slides.source: Source: Spiegel et al., Ann Intern Med, 2004

slides.label: The caveat
slides.title: It is one small study
slides.body: It shows why tired days can feel hungrier. On short-sleep days, plan your snacks before the cravings hit.

slides.text: Better sleep is a skill. Get one tip a day.

posts.title: The best nap is shorter than you think
posts.caption: A 26-minute nap improved pilots' alertness by up to 54% and performance by 34% in a NASA study (1995). #nap #sleeptips #sleep #healthtok #productivity

slides.text: The best nap is shorter than you think

slides.label: The study
slides.title: A 26-minute nap helped pilots
slides.body: In a 1995 NASA study, pilots given a nap opportunity on long flights showed up to 54% better alertness and 34% better performance.
slides.source: Source: NASA pilot nap study, 1995

slides.label: The risk
slides.title: Longer naps can leave you groggy
slides.body: Longer naps are more likely to cause sleep inertia, that dazed, sluggish feeling. Naps of 20 to 30 minutes can boost alertness without significant grogginess.
slides.source: Source: Sleep Foundation, NASA nap

slides.label: Try this
slides.title: Set a timer for 25 minutes
slides.body: Lie down somewhere dark and quiet. Give yourself a few extra minutes to fall asleep.

slides.text: Better sleep is a skill. Get one tip a day.

posts.title: When should night-shift workers drink coffee?
posts.caption: Guidance from CDC NIOSH: caffeine early in the shift, stop several hours before the shift ends. #nightshift #shiftwork #caffeine #sleeptips #healthtok

slides.text: When should night-shift workers drink coffee?

slides.label: The clock
slides.title: Caffeine has a half-life of 5 to 6 hours
slides.body: It takes about 30 minutes to kick in, and in some people it stays in the system much longer.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, Training for Nurses on Shift Work

slides.label: The plan
slides.title: Use it at the start of the shift
slides.body: NIOSH says night workers who rely on caffeine could use it at the beginning of the shift, then stop several hours before the shift ends.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, Training for Nurses on Shift Work

slides.label: The catch
slides.title: Late coffee follows you to bed
slides.body: A cup near the end of a night shift can leave enough caffeine to cause restlessness or waking during your sleep the next morning.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, Training for Nurses on Shift Work

slides.label: Bonus
slides.title: Pair it with a nap
slides.body: In nurse studies, a 2.5-hour nap plus caffeine at the start of the shift had positive effects on alertness.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, Training for Nurses on Shift Work

slides.text: Better sleep is a skill. Get one tip a day.

posts.title: Under 4 hours of sleep: 11.5 times the crash risk
posts.caption: Drivers who slept under 4 hours had 11.5 times the crash risk of those who slept 7 or more hours (AAA Foundation, 2016). If you're very sleepy, don't drive. #sleep #drowsydriving #sleepscience #healthtok #safety

slides.text: Under 4 hours of sleep and your crash risk is 11.5 times higher

slides.label: The study
slides.title: 7,234 drivers in 4,571 crashes
slides.body: The AAA Foundation analyzed a national crash survey and compared crash risk by how much the driver had slept.
slides.source: Source: AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety, 2016

slides.label: The ladder
slides.title: Risk climbs as sleep drops
slides.body: 6–7 hours: 1.3 times. 5–6 hours: 1.9 times. 4–5 hours: 4.3 times. Under 4 hours: 11.5 times.
slides.source: Source: AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety, 2016

slides.label: The point
slides.title: Even one or two hours short matters
slides.body: Sleeping 5–6 hours was linked to nearly double the crash risk compared with 7 or more hours.
slides.source: Source: AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety, 2016

slides.label: Do this
slides.title: If you are very sleepy, do not drive
slides.body: Pull over somewhere safe or let someone else drive. Save the trip for when you have slept.

slides.text: Better sleep is a skill. Get one tip a day.
